Your horse rates fine. He's reading the cattle, reading the barrel. Then the back end just falls out.

You add more practice. He keeps doing it.

Here's what often gets missed: when the joints through the lower back and pelvis are restricted, the horse can't generate the push he needs through the hindquarters — even if he wants to. That quitting feeling isn't attitude. It's a structural problem.

Dr. Leo works with performance horses across DFW and North Texas who are in peak competition season right now. If your horse is leaving runs on the table and you can't find it in the training, it might be time to look somewhere else.

"He started loading slow. Didn't want to step up. I figured he was just being hard-headed — he'd done it fine for years.

Dr. Leo found his whole right side was locked up. Poll, neck, rib. All of it.

First haul after the adjustment, he walked right on."

— North Texas barrel competitor

Horses don't get difficult for no reason. If something changed in how yours behaves — loading, saddling, standing quiet at the gate — that's worth paying attention to.

Five months in.

Your horse has hauled. He's competed. He's earned it every weekend. And most of the time, nobody's actually checked him — just expected him to keep performing.

Late summer is when the accumulated work catches up. Not always dramatic. Sometimes it's just a little short behind, a little resistant to collect, a little slow to load. You notice it. You file it away.

Don't file it away.
